item.title: Perceptual glimpses are locally accumulated and globally maintained at distinct processing levels.
item.description:
eLife
Making decisions often requires the integration of multiple pieces of information. An extensive body of research has investigated the neural architecture underpinning evidence accumulation in perceptual tasks where information is continuously present, but less is known about how this neural architecture operates in situations affording only intermittent glimpses of an evidence source. In two electroencephalography experiments, human participants judged the direction of up to two pulses of motion evidence separated by gaps of varying duration. Our behavioural analysis found that participants used both pulses but underutilised the second and showed no systematic decrease in accuracy as a function of gap duration. At the neural level, motor beta lateralisation tracked cumulative evidence across pulses, maintaining a sustained representation of the decision variable through the gap and until response. In contrast, the centroparietal positivity (CPP), a previously characterised signature of evidence accumulation, built up transiently to a peak that scaled with each pulse's contribution to the decision variable (i.e. the absolute belief update it produced), falling back to baseline in between pulses. These patterns were recapitulated in a model where pulse-information transiently integrated at the CPP level is fed to and maintained at a bounded motor level. In this model, the evidence in the second pulse is only integrated to the extent that the evidence in the first pulse falls short of the bound, or not integrated at all if a bound has already been hit.

item.title: Insulin resistance is associated with lower cerebral myelin content in cognitively unimpaired women across the adult lifespan.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundInsulin resistance (IR) has been implicated in brain aging and Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet its relationship with cerebral myelin content in cognitively unimpaired adults remains unclear, particularly regarding sex differences.ObjectiveTo investigate whether peripheral IR is associated with white matter (WM) myelin content and microstructural integrity in cognitively unimpaired adults, and whether these associations differ by sex.MethodsWe used multicomponent relaxometry (n = 125) and diffusion tensor imaging (n = 116) to obtain myelin water fraction (MWF), longitudinal relaxation rate (R1), transverse relaxation rate (R2), and diffusion measures of WM microstructure. Multiple linear regression models adjusted for age, age2, sex, and IR-by-sex interactions across fifteen WM regions.ResultsHigher IR was associated with lower MWF across widespread WM regions, including frontal, temporal, and parietal lobes, corpus callosum, internal capsule, and thalamic radiation. Similar but weaker negative trends were observed for R1, R2, and fractional anisotropy, whereas diffusivity metrics showed opposite but nonsignificant trends. Significant IR-by-sex interactions indicated stronger inverse associations between IR and MWF in women, in whom higher IR was consistently associated with lower MWF across most regions. However, the dynamic range of IR for men was limited.ConclusionsHigher peripheral IR is associated with lower myelin-sensitive WM MRI measures in cognitively unimpaired adults, with stronger associations in women. These findings identify WM myelin alterations as a potential neurobiological correlate of metabolic dysfunction and provide evidence linking peripheral metabolic dysfunction to brain changes relevant to AD pathophysiology. The findings highlight a potential sex-dependent pathway linking metabolic dysfunction to WM alterations associated with AD risk.

item.title: Early Neural Responses to Negative Emotional Processing and Longitudinal Grief Trajectories in Later Life.
item.description:
Psychotherapy and psychosomatics
INTRODUCTION: While most bereaved adults adapt to their loss within a year, 3-10% develop Prolonged Grief Disorder. The neurobiological substrates of adaptive versus maladaptive grief trajectories remain poorly understood. METHODS: In this longitudinal study, ninety-seven adults (50-83 years) bereaved within the past year completed task-based fMRI (an emotional face-matching paradigm) and resting-state fMRI at study baseline. Grief symptoms were repeatedly assessed over 12 months. Voxel-wise linear mixed-effects models with cluster-wise correction (uncorrected p=.005; alpha=.05) examined associations between baseline fMRI responses to negative emotional faces (fearful and angry) versus shapes and 12-month symptom trajectories, adjusting for demographics, time since loss, and depressive symptoms. RESULTS: At baseline, left anterior insula activity was positively associated with loneliness (r=.305) and intrusive thoughts (r=.328). Longitudinally, greater baseline activity in bilateral anterior insula and left amygdala was associated with faster improvement in loneliness (z<-3.01). Lower amygdala-orbitofrontal cortex resting-state connectivity was associated with faster loneliness improvement, with stronger effects at higher depressive symptoms and greater perceived social support. Conversely, greater left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity (z=3.10) and its task-dependent connectivity with lateral occipital cortices (z=3.18) were associated with slower improvement in avoidant coping. CONCLUSION: Greater engagement of salience network circuit components during negative emotional processing was associated with diminishing loneliness, whereas greater recruitment of prefrontal executive control network node was associated with persistent avoidance. These findings suggest distinct neural pathways underlying adaptive versus maladaptive grief responses. Further research to confirm these observations and to develop early risk stratification and mechanism-informed interventions to prevent prolonged grief is needed.

item.title: The hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine for memory, perception and cognitive dysfunction.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
The hippocampus is a central cognitive hub whose dysfunction contributes to most neurodegenerative dementias. Despite extensive knowledge of its anatomy, physiology and circuitry, a unifying account that links hippocampal dynamics to cognition and clinical syndromes remains lacking. Drawing on systems neuroscience and recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, we conceptualize the hippocampus as a latent diffusion engine that compresses sensory, interoceptive and cognitive inputs into low-dimensional representations and regenerates percepts, episodic memories and imagined scenes for cortical integration. Travelling waves of cortico-hippocampal oscillations, aligned with large-scale functional gradients, schedule and structure this generative process and organize distributed neural activity into coherent, semantically grounded constructs. We formalize this proposal as stochastic latent oscillatory diffusion (SLOD), a biologically grounded framework that maps hippocampal-cortical computations onto specific anatomical substrates and dynamical processes. While we do not suggest that the hippocampus implements diffusion algorithms per se, we show that its computations can be decomposed into homologous operations including compression, stochastic exploration, conditioning and reconstruction, whose formal structure closely parallels that of latent diffusion models. Finally, we demonstrate how major neurodegenerative dementias, including the Alzheimer's disease spectrum, dementia with Lewy bodies and frontotemporal dementia, can be understood as selective breakdowns of distinct components of this generative architecture.

item.title: [Cognitive involvement in adult myotonic dystrophy type 1: new findings from the North].
item.description:
Medecine sciences : M/S
Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is the most common adult-onset myopathy, but is also a brain disorder leading to cognitive impairment. This brain condition remains poorly characterized: the scientific literature highlighted different cognitive profiles, and no predominant mechanism has been identified. Recent findings from our team in Lille, France, help to better understand this cognitive impairment. We showed that three distinct cognitive profiles exist, patients probably starting from the least severe to the most severe profile with ageing, while brain abnormalities progress in the anterior regions of the brain (frontal and parietal lobes). Despite this cognitive heterogeneity, some difficulties seemed more frequent in our patients, especially those concerning social cognition (skills especially involved in social interactions), and might be explained by white matter lesions in the temporal poles, but also by neurodevelopmental abnormalities in the right parietal lobe.

item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication.
item.description:
eLife
The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f ) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f 4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.title: Genetic, neural and early-environmental architecture of resilience
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.

item.title: Reduced Resting Brain Entropy and Structural-Functional Reorganization in Hearing Loss
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Hearing loss changes how the brain processes sound, yet how chronic auditory degradation shapes the temporal organization of spontaneous cortical activity remains unclear. We examined this question using multimodal MRI from 52 adults with age-related hearing loss and 30 normal-hearing controls. Guided by convergent neuroimaging evidence, we focused on the superior temporal gyrus (STG) and assessed brain entropy (BEN), complementary resting-state measures, and gray matter volume (GMV). Hearing loss was associated with lower BEN in a focal right-STG cluster after adjustment for local GMV (14 voxels; cluster FWER p = 0.008), consistent with more recurrent BOLD signal patterns. Six complementary measures of signal amplitude, local synchrony, symbolic sequence diversity, successive variation, and temporal persistence showed no corrected STG differences. A separate whole-brain analysis revealed higher bilateral midcingulate cortex (MCC) GMV (FWE p = 0.002 and 0.015), motivating examination of the auditory-cingulate relationship. The BEN-defined STG region showed stronger focal functional connectivity with MCC (FWE p = 0.031). Exploratory analyses suggested weaker directed STG-to-MCC influence alongside a small tractography-derived group difference. Exploratory directional comparisons indicated stronger right-MCC GMV-BEN coupling (p = 0.034) and STG-MCC SC-FC coupling (p = 0.037) in controls than in hearing loss. Together, these findings link greater temporal regularity in auditory association cortex to altered auditory-cingulate coordination and local structure-function correspondence, suggesting that adaptation to hearing loss involves both the organization of spontaneous cortical dynamics and their relationship to brain structure.

item.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control ( d ′ context; η 2 p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; η 2 p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.

item.title: Dance experience shapes local brain dynamics and shared responses during naturalistic action observation
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Skilled action observation unfolds over time: viewers follow changing movements, coordinate what they see with prior experience, and form a response to the performance as a whole. Dance expertise is known to alter action-related activation and the similarity of spectators' responses, but its association with local BOLD dynamics during an extended performance remains unclear. We reanalyzed fMRI from 14 professional dancers and 11 novices watching the same 33-minute dance film; one choreographer provided a separate reference. In the first 678 volumes, we measured voxelwise brain entropy (BEN) using sample entropy before summarizing it in Schaefer 400 parcels and seven networks, calculated windowed entropy from parcel-mean signals, and examined intersubject correlation (ISC) and four group-blind coactivation patterns (CAPs). After adjustment for local gray-matter volume, age, sex, and motion, dancers had higher static BEN in 32 parcels and six networks (FDR q < .05). Dynamic BEN was higher in control and default-mode networks. Dancer-dancer ISC exceeded novice-novice ISC in five networks. Dancers occupied one common CAP less often and another more often, while performer synchrony and acceleration tracked state occurrence across spectators. These converging observations show that dance experience is expressed in local temporal irregularity, shared spectator responses, and the distribution of brain states during naturalistic action observation.

item.title: White Matter Pathway-Specific Effects of Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation on Vergence Motor Strategy and Binocular Stability
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: Clear vision across viewing distances requires the eyes to achieve binocular alignment and hold it steady. Alignment can be established through smooth dysconjugate eye movement, vergence, alone or in conjunction with rapid saccades. The circuits governing movement strategy and subsequent gaze holding remain less understood. Methods: We used subthalamic nucleus (STN) deep brain stimulation (DBS) to probe these components in 23 participants with Parkinson disease (PD), comparing binocular eye movements with stimulation on and off and relating behavioral changes to modeled stimulation anatomy. Results: Combined saccade vergence responses predominated in both stimulation states, but individual strategy changes were associated with stimulation location. Greater field of Forel coverage was associated with reduced saccade assisted divergence, and stimulation anatomy helped predict individual changes in this movement strategy. Greater right associative STN coverage correlated with shorter convergence latency. The clearest group effect emerged after movement ended; DBS reduced gaze-holding variance by 37.0% after convergence and 29.4% after divergence, an overall reduction of 33.3% (95% confidence interval, 13.7 to 49.3%; p=0.008). Participants with improved gaze holding had numerically greater modeled exposure to Forel and cerebellothalamic pathways. Conclusions: These findings suggest distinct contributions of associative STN to initiation, consistent with go/no-go control, and Forel pathways to movement strategy. Improved gaze holding raises the novel possibility that stimulation engaging Forel and cerebellar outflow pathways enhances vergence neural integration. Significance: Binocular eye movements reveal how basal ganglia and cerebellar pathways establish movement strategy and sustain alignment, guiding targeted stimulation studies in PD.

item.title: Changes in Resting-State Functional Network Specialization in Progressive Supranuclear Palsy
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a neurodegenerative tauopathy characterized by heterogeneous clinical presentations and disruption of distributed neural networks. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) provides a systems-level approach to examine intrinsic brain connectivity and may offer insights into disease-related network dysfunction. In this study, we compared rs-fMRI connectivity measures between individuals with PSP and healthy controls and explored differences across PSP clinical variants. 23 participants with probable or possible PSP and 23 age- and sex-matched healthy controls underwent structural and functional MRI. Graph theory metrics and functional connectivity measures across seven canonical resting-state networks were analyzed. Clinical severity was assessed using the PSP Rating Scale (PSPRS) and cognitive measures including the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and frontal assessment battery (FAB). Compared with controls, participants with PSP demonstrated significantly reduced global network modularity and segregation, indicating decreased functional network specialization. Functional connectivity was significantly reduced in multiple large-scale networks, including frontoparietal control, default mode, dorsal attention, somatomotor, and visual networks. No significant differences in graph theory metrics or network connectivity were observed between PSP clinical variants. These findings suggest that PSP is associated with widespread disruption of intrinsic functional networks, reflected by reduced modular organization and network segregation across several canonical resting-state systems while preserving local nodal clustering and global efficiency. Network-level alterations appear broadly similar across clinical variants, supporting the concept that PSP represents a distributed network disorder.

item.title: Brain Signal Variability and Brain-Behavior Coupling in Adults with Dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Background: Brain signal variability indexed by fMRI has emerged as a promising transdiagnostic biomarker for neurodevelopmental disorders, demonstrating better predictive utility than time-averaged metrics for diagnosis, yet it remains underexplored in adult dyslexia. The Neural Noise Hypothesis of dyslexia proposes that genetic risk disrupts cortical excitation/inhibition balance, elevating neural noise and affecting processes essential for reading. Here, we examine resting-state fMRI BOLD variability, a metric linked to neural noise, in adults with dyslexia and investigate its links with behavior. Methods: In 30 adults with dyslexia (DY) and 76 typical readers (TR), we computed three complementary BOLD variability metrics: standard deviation (SD) and mean squared successive differences (MSSD) to quantify BOLD amplitude fluctuations, and dynamic regional homogeneity (dReHo) to quantify local temporal coordination. Voxel-wise group comparisons and partial least squares correlation analyses examined brain-behavior associations across a comprehensive behavioral battery spanning reading (e.g., word reading, phonological processing), math, oral language, working memory, and executive function domains. Results: DY showed higher SD and MSSD in the left ventral occipitotemporal pathway and higher MSSD in the cerebellum, whereas TR showed higher dReHo in frontal and temporoparietal regions. SD/MSSD in visual, somatomotor, cerebellar, and subcortical networks significantly covaried with multi-domain behavioral profiles. Conclusions: Adults with dyslexia showed localized, metric-specific differences in brain signal variability and brain-behavior covariance, indicating region-specific rather than global alterations. These results suggest that brain signal variability is a promising candidate task-free phenotype that could potentially index target engagement in interventions for adult dyslexia.

item.title: Social Connection: Resting-State Functional Connectivity Associations with Social Networks, and the Roles of Empathy and Sex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Smaller social networks (SNs) negatively influence cognition, psychiatric trajectories and mortality. Studies linking SNs to resting-state functional connectivity (FC) inconsistently suggest orbito-frontal and frontoparietal regions and implicate a potential role for empathy and sex. We investigate how SN characteristics relate to FC, additionally assessing if empathy and sex alter these associations. Group-independent component analysis was applied to multi-band resting-state fMRI from 83 participants (Caltech Conte dataset: ds003798). The Social Network Index measures SN-contacts (SN-contacts) SN-diversity (number of roles) and SN-embeddedness (number of contact groups) and the Empathy Quotient measured empathy. Using MANCOVA, we investigate if resting-state network power and connectivity are associated with SNI measures and whether these relationships differ by empathizing ability and sex. Participants aged 18-48 (mean age 29.3+/-7.0, 55% male) demonstrated SN-contacts and SN-diversity associated with lower frontal-pole FC within the default-mode network (DMN, q-values<0.05). Empathy altered how SN-diversity and SN-contacts relate to superior lateral-occipital, default mode and salience network FC (q-values<0.05). Finally, males and females showed diverging associations of SN-contacts and SN-diversity with salience network power. Smaller SNs were associated with increased anterior-DMN FC, potentially indicating a tendency towards internally-directed cognition in more socially isolated individuals. Opposing relationships between SNs with salience and lateral-frontoparietal networks by empathy level highlights empathy as critical for understanding social biology. Males and females differed in SN associations with salience network coherency, supporting known sex-specific neural correlates of social behavior. These findings provide insights into the biology of social networks, offering potential targets for studying social deficits in psychiatric populations.

item.title: Neurocognitive signatures of intrinsic motivation in naturalistic information seeking and memory
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Humans often seek information without direct external reward. Theories distinguish two major dimensions of this intrinsic motivation: wanting, the desire to resolve an information gap, and liking, the enjoyment of the information itself. However, how these motivational dimensions shape self-guided information-seeking behavior, neural activity, and memory formation in realworld contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a naturalistic fMRI paradigm in which participants freely browsed the internet, subsequently recalled their browsing experiences, and retrospectively reported their moment-to-moment wanting and liking. We found that both dimensions predicted more stable browsing trajectories but engaged partially dissociable neural systems: wanting recruited regions supporting goal-directed cognition, whereas liking engaged affective regions. Wanting and liking also interacted to predict memory, with wanting predicting recall primarily when liking was low. Compared with active browsing, passive viewing of the same web content reduced wanting and liking and diminished their dissociation, yet both continued to predict memory and intersubject neural similarity in the default mode network. These findings show that naturally fluctuating wanting and liking guide how we seek and remember information through overlapping yet distinct neurocognitive mechanisms.

item.title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.

item.title: Neural tracking of phonological, lexical, and syntactic surprisal during naturalistic listening in elementary-aged children with and without dyslexia
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Children with dyslexia show persistent phonological difficulties in controlled experiments yet often comprehend everyday spoken language successfully. The present study examined how children with and without dyslexia neurally track phonological, lexical, and syntactic information during naturalistic story listening, and how this tracking relates to reading proficiency. Children listened to a story during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Study 1 examined neural tracking in 140 typically developing (TD) children. Study 2 compared children with dyslexia with age- and gender-matched TD controls (n = 35 per group). Large language model-derived surprisal estimates indexed tracking at each level at exploratory and multiple comparison corrected thresholds. In TD children, each level of surprisal tracking showed a distinct cortical profile, and higher reading comprehension was associated with greater phonological and syntactic tracking, but reduced lexical tracking. Children with dyslexia also showed distinct tracking profiles across levels. In this group, however, higher reading proficiency was associated with greater lexical and syntactic tracking and reduced phonological tracking. Group contrasts mirrored these patterns. Children with and without dyslexia differ in how neural tracking of linguistic information relates to reading. In dyslexia, reduced phonological tracking alongside greater lexical tracking may reflect increased reliance on higher-level linguistic information. Syntactic tracking was positively related to reading proficiency in both groups, consistent with the protracted development of syntax and its contribution to literacy. These findings offer new insights into the real-time neurobiology of naturalistic language comprehension and how the interaction of underlying skills may vary in children with dyslexia.

item.title: Bridging brain structure and function: Structural-functional brain network coupling and frontal midline theta connectivity in general intelligence
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Structural connectivity (SC) and functional connectivity (FC), as well as their alignment (SC-FC coupling), may underlie individual differences in general intelligence. We hypothesized that intelligence emerges from optimized SC-FC coupling and additional processes, namely the task-dependent rapid regulation of FC. To test this hypothesis, we examined MRI-derived SC-FC coupling and EEG-derived midfrontal theta FC dynamics as complementary predictors of intelligence within a latent variable framework. We used a sample of 215 healthy adults (113 females) aged 18–40 years who underwent extensive cognitive ability testing and completed a conceptually similar cued task-switching task during EEG and functional MRI acquisition. Although we found no evidence for a broad association between whole-brain SC-FC coupling and intelligence, an exploratory analysis contrasting functional contexts revealed one for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling computed from task-evoked FC. Specifically, higher coupling predicted higher general intelligence, β = 0.28, 95% CI [0.09, 0.47]. Regarding midfrontal theta connectivity, we found no evidence for an association with intelligence at a preregistered electrode (Fz). However, an exploratory analysis of a broader electrode cluster revealed a temporally specific effect, β = 0.36, 95% CI [0.05, 0.67], suggesting that intelligence may rely on flexible modulation of FC across successive stages of information processing. In a combined model, the two connectivity-based predictors showed no substantial correlation with each other, r = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.10, 0.25], but both remained significant predictors of intelligence, β = 0.26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.45] for frontoparietal SC-FC coupling and β = 0.22, 95% CI [0.06, 0.39] for late midfrontal theta connectivity. Together, both predictors explained 12.7% of variance in intelligence differences. These findings highlight that the connectivity–intelligence association may be spatially and temporally specific, while emphasizing that intelligence relies on multiple connectivity mechanisms spanning the brain’s structure and function.

item.title: Intervening contexts reshape hippocampal-cortical retrieval states and later source attribution.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Memories are often reactivated in one context and only later judged with respect to where they originally occurred. We tested how an intervening retrieval context shapes neural representations and later source memory. In two fMRI tasks, participants (both male and female) encoded objects within contextual backgrounds, completed an immediate retrieval test in which object cues appeared against either the original background or a different background, and subsequently judged each object's original context on a neutral screen. Shifted cueing contexts reduced source accuracy and biased errors toward the intervening context, despite no detectable difference in immediate recognition or associative-memory performance. Representational similarity analyses showed that encoding patterns reflected original-context structure, whereas immediate-cue-period patterns were broadly organized by the cued (i.e., currently visible) context. On shifted trials, activity patterns showed greater similarity to encoding-derived templates for the cued context than for the original context. Across participants, greater differentiation of original-context similarity between consistent and shifted cueing in posterior hippocampus, parahippocampal cortex, and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex was associated with better source memory after a contextual shift. Within participants, precuneus contextual engagement and dorsal anterior cingulate context alignment predicted later source choices, with similar relationships after adjustment for immediate recognition responses. Later source attribution therefore depended on the contextual state expressed when an item was re-encountered, not simply on reinstatement of the original event.Significance statement Remembering is often described as bringing up the past, but memories are frequently reactivated in new contexts before we judge where they came from. We show that this intervening context can bias later source attribution even when that context is no longer visible at final test. Using two fMRI tasks, representational similarity analysis and trial-level source-choice models, we found that cue-period activity was organized by the context present during cueing and that specific context-state signals predicted later memory choices, whereas item reinstatement did not. Source-memory errors can therefore reflect contextual information encountered after the original event, not only failures to recover the original context.

item.title: Multidimensional dynamics of object representations in the human visual system.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Natural image representations are distributed across many dimensions of visual cortex activity, but little is known about how the multidimensional structure of these representations evolves over time following stimulus onset. Herewe examined the temporal dynamics and latent dimensional structure of natural object representations in large-scale EEG and MEG data from male and female human participants. We also compared these datawith leading representational models derived from large-scale human similarity judgments and deep neural networks. Our findings reveal a rapid expansion of stimulus dimensionality in the brain, which peaks within 100 milliseconds and gradually decays over hundreds of milliseconds. The dynamics of these dimensionality changes tracked the decoding accuracy for both behavioral embeddings and neural network features, suggesting that dimensionality may be a general indicator of representational expressivity. Interestingly, the dimensionality of the neural representations could not be fully explained by a leading behavior-based model or deep neural network. Follow-up experiments showed that the remaining neural variance carried additional perceptually relevant information not yet explained by leading models. Together, these findings reveal previously unrecognized complexity in measurements of dynamic human brain responses to natural objects.Significance Statement When we look at an object, our brains rapidly construct a rich internal representation of what we see. Using large-scale, time-resolved brain recordings from people viewing thousands of natural images, we find that the brain rapidly expands its representational complexity within the first 100 milliseconds, sustaining this richness for hundreds of milliseconds thereafter. A leading behavioral model and a large-scale deep neural network do not fully account for this complexity - yet the unexplained brain activity is not noise: people can reliably use these residual neural patterns to judge image similarity. These findings challenge the assumption that such brain recordings are informationally limited and reveal structure in the human visual system that future models will need to explain.

item.title: Motor system inefficiency as an activity-dependent amplifier of fatigue in multiple sclerosis.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Multiple sclerosis (MS) fatigue is clinically obvious but mechanistically elusive. It can dominate daily life despite modest disability, stable structural MRI findings, or preserved strength on examination. This Update reviews evidence that an important component of MS fatigue may arise from increased motor-control cost and incomplete recovery after activity. Voluntary muscle activation studies show that some people with MS have incomplete central access to available force, particularly after exertion. Functional imaging studies indicate that apparently preserved movement often depends on expanded recruitment of premotor, cerebellar, striatal, prefrontal, and cingulo-insular systems involved in motor compensation, effort allocation, and body-state monitoring. Metabolic and pathological studies further indicate energetic vulnerability in demyelinated and chronically injured networks, providing biological plausibility for impaired restoration after repeated signalling demands. These findings support a systems framework in which expanded motor-control recruitment may be compensatory when it preserves performance and remains flexible and recoverable, but may amplify MS fatigue when ordinary activity begins from incompletely restored physiological reserve. We outline testable predictions for identifying a motor-cost fatigue phenotype and for designing repeated-measures studies of activity-related fatigue in MS.

item.title: Chronic and subacute phenylalanine effects on brain metabolism in adults with phenylketonuria.
item.description:
Brain : a journal of neurology
Phenylketonuria (PKU) leads to chronic cerebral exposure to elevated phenylalanine (Phe) despite lifelong dietary treatment, yet the neurometabolic consequences in adulthood remain incompletely understood. We investigated whether adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent alterations in brain metabolism and whether these metabolites respond dynamically to subacute Phe fluctuations. Adults with early-treated PKU (n=30) and healthy controls (n=59) underwent proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H-MRS), structural and functional brain MRI to evaluate white matter lesion load (T2-weighted images) and cerebral blood flow (arterial spin labeling), as well as cognitive assessments. Patients additionally participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover intervention with four weeks of oral Phe loading to evaluate subacute metabolic responsiveness. Absolute metabolite concentrations were quantified in predominantly white matter tissue, and associations between blood and brain Phe, white matter lesion load, cerebral blood flow, and cognitive performance were examined. At baseline, patients exhibited higher brain Phe and N-acetylaspartate (NAA) levels, alongside reduced myo-inositol, N-acetylaspartylglutamate (NAAG), and total creatine/phosphocreatine compared with controls. Patients with white matter lesions did not differ in blood and brain metabolites from those without. Four weeks of oral Phe loading increased brain Phe and produced a reversible decrease in myo-inositol, whereas NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds remained unchanged. Blood and brain Phe concentrations were strongly correlated (r=0.83, p<0.001), and their ratio was subject-dependent. No significant associations were observed between metabolite concentrations and regional cerebral blood flow or cognitive performance after correction for multiple comparisons. Adults with early-treated PKU exhibit persistent neurometabolic alterations involving neuronal-glial metabolism, energy buffering, and astrocytic osmolyte regulation. The findings support a trait-state framework, with stable alterations in NAA, NAAG, and creatine compounds reflecting long-standing metabolic changes, superimposed on a dynamically Phe-sensitive astrocytic response indexed by myo-inositol. The absence of strong associations with cerebral perfusion or cognition suggests that these alterations represent upstream biological processes not captured by macroscopic imaging or behavioral measures.

item.title: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects.
item.description:
Nature communications
Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

item.title: Beyond memory strengthening: noradrenergic control of memory specificity.
item.description:
Trends in neurosciences
Emotionally significant events are typically remembered better and for longer than mundane experiences. This emotional memory enhancement critically depends on arousal-induced norepinephrine release within the brain. Beyond memory strengthening, recent work shows that noradrenergic activity also shapes the specificity, detailedness, and temporal precision of memories during both early consolidation and systems consolidation. In this review, we synthesize recent findings from human and animal research spanning molecular, circuit, systems, and behavioral mechanisms to propose an integrative framework for how emotional arousal-induced noradrenergic activity affects neural systems that regulate memory specificity and systems consolidation dynamics. The proposed framework refines current models of memory under emotional arousal and may have relevant implications for stress-related psychopathologies.

item.title: Ultra-low-field MRI assesses brain volumes and age-related changes: validation against high-field MRI.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
High-field MRI is the standard for assessing brain atrophy in neurodegenerative disorders, but limited access can restrict research and clinical care, particularly outside urban centers. Portable ultra-low-field (ULF) MRI may improve access, but their suitability for quantitative morphometry and detection of neurodegenerative-related atrophy is not well established. We evaluated agreement between 64 mT ULF MRI and 3T MRI for brain volumetric measurements and explored their potential utility in neurodegenerative disorders. We conducted a prospective, cross-sectional study of adults, including patients with neurodegenerative, subacute stroke, and healthy controls. Participants underwent both 3T and 64 mT ULF MRI with T1-weighted imaging. Regional brain volumes were extracted from both modalities using WMH-SynthSeg. Agreement between ULF- and 3T-derived volumes were assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients and Bland-Altman analyses. Where applicable, 3T FreeSurfer-derived volumes were used as an additional reference standard. Analyses in the neurodegenerative disorder subgroup were considered exploratory because the subgroup was not powered for formal inferential comparisons. ULF and 3T volumetric measures show variable agreement (ICC ranged from 0.29 to 0.95), with the highest agreement for large structures such as total ventricles (ICC 0.85 to 0.95) and the lowest for the Pallidum (ICC 0.34 to 0.51). Age-related trajectories of gray and white matter decline, and ventricular expansion show the same pattern for WMH-SynthSeg and FreeSurfer-derived volumes. Exploratory analysis suggests pathological atrophy might differ from healthy aging trajectories. Portable ultra-low-field MRI combined with automated segmentation produced brain volumetric estimates that were broadly consistent with 3T MRI, particularly for larger structures relevant to atrophy assessment. These findings support the feasibility of ultra-low-field MRI for accessible morphometric evaluation in clinical research and potentially in under-resourced settings. Larger, adequately powered studies are needed to define diagnostic accuracy, prediction intervals, and clinical utility in specific neurodegenerative disorder populations.

item.title: A theory of generalized vector coding and subicular function.
item.description:
Current biology : CB
Neural information processing is inextricably linked to the selectivity of individual neurons, as described by their receptive fields. Far from the sensory periphery, neural representations are the result of substantial upstream processing, mixed with internally generated information. Low-dimensional spatial codes in the hippocampal formation offer a handle on understanding these representations. The subiculum, a key but comparatively understudied hippocampal area, exhibits numerous, seemingly unrelated neural codes. Neurons like boundary vector cells, corner cells, or axis-tuned cells are named after the environmental features that appear to drive them, but a common account for their neuronal selectivity is lacking. Here, we propose Disco, a theory explaining subicular functions and related neural codes in other areas. Given the continuous flow of experience, subicular activity can be understood as signaling discontinuities in that flow, coded in a vector base. Geometric discontinuities drive responses to walls, drops, objects, holes, corners, and curved surfaces. The generality of Disco enables predictions for 3D environments, natural scenes, and mixed-modality coding. Discontinuities are not identical to the concept of boundaries (abstract or spatial), as illustrated by non-spatial discontinuities in behavioral state. These yield axis coding in the model (activity along parallel maze arms). Finally, tracking population activity signals event boundaries as discontinuities in neural space. The emergence of diverse neural activity suggests that discontinuity coding may serve as a key principle in the subiculum and related brain areas supporting (spatial) memory and navigation.

item.title: The level of cortical thickening in executive functions and audiovisual integration regions predicts reading comprehension via reading fluency in musically experienced children.
item.description:
Brain research
Proficient reading fluency, which is critical for intact reading comprehension, is related to efficient audio-visual integration and to executive functions (EF). Interestingly, musical training has been associated with better audio-visual integration, EF, and reading abilities. However, the direct relationship, cognitively and neurobiologically, between these components remains ambiguous. Here, we examined the neurobiological correlates of the predictive role of EF and audio-visual integration on reading comprehension through fluency in children with and without music experience using cortical thickness (CT) measures. A high-resolution T1-weighted anatomical scan was acquired from 8- to 12-year-old children with and without music experience. CT within EF (anterior cingulate cortex) and audio-visual (insula) brain regions was compared between groups. A moderated mediation analysis was conducted with anterior cingulate cortex CT as the predictor variable, reading comprehension as the outcome variable, reading fluency as the mediator, and music experience as the moderator, with age and sex as covariates. Musically inexperienced children demonstrated lower reading fluency, comprehension, and EF abilities compared to experienced children. In experienced children, CT in the anterior cingulate gyrus predicted comprehension via an indirect pathway mediated by fluency (B = 21.63, BootSE = 9.11, 95 % CI [4.56, 40.85]); in inexperienced children, neither the direct nor indirect pathways significantly predicted comprehension (B = 11.53, BootSE = 8.64, 95 % CI [-6.54, 28.80]). The Index of Moderated Mediation was not significant (IMM = - 10.10, BootSE = 11.79, 95 % CI [-34.92, 12.21]); thus, there was no statistical evidence that the indirect effect differed between the groups. Results suggest that musical experience is associated with differences in neural circuits linked to EF and audiovisual integration, which in turn relate to reading fluency and comprehension.

item.title: Functional connectivity profile of the amygdala subfields associates with emotional well-being in aging.
item.description:
GeroScience
Amygdala-related functional connectivity (FC) plays a crucial role in human emotion, cognition, and mental well-being. The amygdala is a highly heterogeneous structure, with subregions that have both distinct and overlapping functions. However, the connectivity patterns of different amygdala subregions, and how these associations vary with age, remain poorly understood. Functional MRI data were analyzed from 68 younger adults and 66 older adults during movie watching in a 7-T MRI scanner. Partial least squares (PLS) analysis was used to identify latent variables capturing variance associated with age-related differences in the FC patterns of three amygdala subregions: the basolateral (BLA), centromedial (CMA), and superficial (SFA) nuclei. In addition, covariance between behavioral measures, including emotional resilience and cognitive function, and FC of these subregions were examined. We further explored correspondence with large-scale brain networks, the associated cognitive processes in Neurosynth, and the spatial distributions of neurotransmitter receptors of the identified connectivity patterns of the BLA, CMA, and SFA. Multivariate analyses revealed that functional connectivity patterns of amygdala subregions related to emotional resilience largely overlapped across widespread brain regions; however, their associations differed by age. During negative movie viewing, stronger coupling of amygdala subregions with the cortex were associated with higher emotional resilience in older adults but lower emotional resilience in younger adults. Associations with cognitive function were weaker and less consistent across subregions. The identified connectivity patterns were linked to the salience, control, and default mode networks and showed spatial correspondence with mGluR5 and 5-HT6 receptor distributions. These findings highlight age-dependent reorganization of amygdala-related networks that support emotional resilience and provide novel insights into the functional connectivity patterns associated with emotional well-being in younger and older adults.

item.title: A multi-subject tractography atlas of human cerebellar connections.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The cerebellum is a highly interconnected structure involved in motor coordination and balance as well as cognitive, sensory, autonomic, and emotional functions. Its connectivity relies on complex afferent and efferent white matter pathways linking it with the brainstem, spinal cord, thalamus, cerebral cortex, vestibular system, and limbic-related structures. Recent advances in diffusion MRI (dMRI) and tractography have enabled the in vivo reconstruction of these pathways, offering new opportunities to study cerebellar anatomy and connectivity. However, compared with supratentorial white matter, cerebellar connections remain underexplored owing to their smaller size, anatomical complexity, and the absence of comprehensive tractography atlases. We propose a white matter tractography atlas of candidate cerebellar white matter pathways, consistent with previously reported neuroanatomical descriptions based on regions of interest (ROIs) derived from 30 young healthy volunteers from the Human Connectome Project (HCP). A total of 22 ROIs were segmented to reconstruct, via tractography, 19 cerebellum-associated tractography components, comprising eight bilateral pathways (16 hemisphere-specific reconstructions), and the three major cerebellar white matter conduits: the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles (SCP, MCP, and ICP). The eight bilateral pathways comprise the cerebello-ponto-hypothalamic, parieto-ponto-cerebellar, fronto-ponto-cerebellar, occipito-ponto-cerebellar, contralateral cerebello-thalamo-cortical, dentato-rubro-thalamo-cortical, dorsal spinocerebellar, and periaqueductal gray-cerebellar pathways. The delineation of some anatomical regions, particularly the olivary nucleus and the hypothalamus, presented methodological challenges. Difficulties in reliably reconstructing the olivocerebellar pathway led to its exclusion from the final atlas. Two independent neuroanatomical experts evaluated the 19 atlas tracts using four qualitative criteria, finding good anatomical fidelity with overall mean scores of 3.9 and 3.8 out of 5, respectively. The same reconstruction procedure was then applied to 25 additional HCP participants to evaluate the automatic segmentation of these bundles in unseen participants. The proposed atlas provides a framework for studying putative cerebellar structural connectivity, acknowledging that tractography-derived streamlines represent inferred white matter pathways rather than direct evidence of synaptic connections or axonal trajectories and its relationship with motor and non-motor functions. It enables quantitative tractometry analyses derived from diffusion MRI models and facilitates the integration of multimodal and functional information. This atlas may support future research in neuroscience, neuropsychiatric disorders, and neurosurgical planning by providing a standardized representation of cerebellar white matter pathways.

item.title: Longitudinal examination of cerebellar morphometry across typical aging adults reveals nonlinear heterogenous trends
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cerebellar structural integrity has been associated with cognitive capability in both neurodegenerative and healthy aging populations. The understanding of regional, longitudinal cerebellar structural changes is not well studied, and with an increasing aging population, there is an increasing need to fill this gap. Moreover, traditional modeling approaches apply linear techniques, which may fail to detect possible nuanced aging patterns. The present study investigates the nonlinear effect of age on subregional cerebellar structures in healthy adults (n = 1,371), aged 36 to 90+, from the Human Connectome Project in Aging and the follow-up continuation, Aging Adult Brain Connectome studies. Subject T1w images underwent cerebellar segmentation and volumetric estimation via the Automatic Cerebellum Parcellation using U-NET with Locally Constrained Optimization (ACAPULCO) algorithm. Cross-sectional, longitudinal, and sex specific volumetric differences were examined using generalized additive mixed models. Heterogenous atrophy patterns were observed across the cerebellum; however, the majority of effects were evident in the posterior cerebellum. Longitudinal models showed nonlinear negative trends for all regions surviving correction, while baseline age effects had a combination of linear and nonlinear negative trajectories after correction. Specific sex differences emerged, where men predominantly had higher regional volumes, as well as there being sex-related influences of longitudinal morphologic patterns. Furthermore, midlife appeared as a period of structural vulnerability, demonstrating escalated volume loss. Consistent with the literature, the identified volumetric reduction patterns suggest that age effects on the cerebellum are multifaceted, with region specific alterations, highlighting the complexity of this structure.

item.title: Partially shared representational space for vision and language across objects, scenes, and visual events
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Deep neural networks (DNNs) and behavioural similarity judgements of visual stimuli predict neural responses in visual cortex. Recent work shows that large language model (LLM) embeddings and similarity judgements of language descriptions also predict visual brain activity. These predictors were examined separately across modalities (vision vs language) and types (models vs human behaviour). It remains unclear to what extent these predictors explain shared or unique aspects of visual brain responses, how these contributions vary along the visual hierarchy and category-selective regions, and whether vision-language convergence depends on the stimulus type. We used three fMRI datasets progressing toward naturalistic visual experience, from objects (THINGS) to scenes (NSD) to dynamic events (BMD). For each dataset, we collected similarity judgements of visual stimuli and of their language descriptions from human participants (N = 21-35), extracted vision DNN features and LLM embeddings, and related similarity judgements and model representations to visual brain responses using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and variance partitioning. Vision-language convergence was higher within behaviour than within models. From objects to dynamic events, LLM alignment with vision-based similarity judgements increased, whereas vision DNN alignment remained stable. A shared, predominantly cross-modal component increased along the visual hierarchy and dominated explained variance in high-level visual cortex. LLMs made their largest unique contributions in face- and body-selective regions (FFA and EBA), where shared representations of vision- and language-based human similarity judgements also explained variance beyond the models. In summary, we find a partially shared representational space for vision and language in high-level visual cortex, most clearly in regions representing social information related to people and their actions. As each predictor retained unique variance, combining computational models and human behaviour across vision and language may offer a more comprehensive account of high-level visual representations.

item.title: Bullying Victimisation, Medial Occipital White Matter Development, and Psychotic-Like Experiences: A Longitudinal Diffusion MRI Study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Childhood bullying victimisation is robustly associated with psychotic-like experiences, but the neurodevelopmental mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear. This longitudinal study examined whether childhood bullying victimisation was associated with altered maturation of medial occipital white matter and whether bullying victimisation moderated the association between fractional anisotropy (FA) and psychotic-like experiences. A total of 96 young people (38 bullied, 58 controls) from the Adolescent Brain Development study underwent diffusion MRI at approximately 14, 16, and 20 years of age. PLE and bullying victimisation group classification were determined by expert consensus interview. FA from bilateral calcarine-cuneus, cuneus-lingual, and calcarine-lingual connections was examined using mixed-effects models. Compared with controls, the bullied group showed significantly different age-related FA trajectories in the right calcarine-cuneus connection (β = -0.40, p < .001) and the left cuneus-lingual connection (β = -0.35, p = .003). Bullying victimisation significantly moderated the association between white matter FA and PLE (β = -6.14, p = .004), indicating that the association between FA and psychotic-like experiences differed according to bullying victimisation status. This moderation effect also varied with age, as indicated by a significant bullying victimisation-by-FA-by-time interaction (β = -6.80, p = .008). Specifically, the moderating effect of bullying victimisation on the association between right calcarine-cuneus FA and PLE changed across development. These findings suggest that bullying victimisation is associated with divergent maturation of medial occipital circuitry and identify right calcarine-cuneus development as a potential marker of vulnerability to PLE following childhood bullying.

item.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Cannabis use disorder (CUD) frequently co-occurs with depressive symptoms, yet shared underlying neurobiological mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the role of depressive symptoms in the relationship between CUD, cannabis use characteristics, and within-network resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) in the Executive Control (ECN), the Salience (SN), the Default Mode (DMN), and the Basal Ganglia (BGN) networks. Methods: In a pooled sample of 132 CUD participants and 102 controls, we examined the associations of group, depressive symptoms, and their interaction with within-network RSFC. Within the CUD group, we assessed the associations between cannabis use characteristics, depressive symptoms, and RSFC. We also conducted an exploratory, non-preregistered sensitivity analysis in the largest contributing study (n = 187). Results: In the full sample and the largest study, depressive symptoms were associated with higher RSFC in the left ECN and interacted with group in the right ECN, showing a positive association between depressive symptoms and RECN RSFC in controls, but not in CUD individuals. The largest study analysis additionally showed lower dorsal SN and higher BGN RSFC in CUD individuals relative to controls. Within the full CUD sample, depressive symptoms were positively associated with anterior SN RSFC among individuals with heavier cannabis use, but negatively among those with lighter use. Conclusion: CUD, heaviness of cannabis use, and depressive symptoms may concurrently relate to RSFC alterations within distinct networks. Group differences potentially emerge at higher levels of CUD and depression severity. This highlights the importance of accounting for depressive symptoms in neurobiological research on CUD.

item.title: Cannabis Use Disorder and Depressive Symptoms: A within-network resting-state functional connectivity study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
