item.title: Frequency-Specific Thalamocortical Network Dynamics During Focal Seizures in Humans.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives The thalamus is an emerging neuromodulation target in drug-resistant focal epilepsy because of its frequent ictal involvement. However, frequency-specific and directional thalamocortical dynamics remain poorly understood. We sought to characterize thalamocortical network dynamics across seizure evolution using stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). Methods We retrospectively analyzed SEEG recordings from patients with pediatric-onset drug-resistant focal epilepsy with simultaneous cortical and thalamic sampling focusing on the anterior nucleus (AN) and centromedian nucleus (CM). We applied visual analysis with quantitative measures of spectral power, imaginary coherence, and spectral Granger causality across slow (1-12 Hz), β (13-30 Hz), and γ (30-70 Hz) bands to quantify thalamocortical and cortico-cortical interactions from seizure onset to termination. Random forest models were trained to classify seizure state using thalamic EEG features as an exploratory analysis. Results The final cohort comprised 19 patients (median age, 16.9 years; 31.6% female), with 66 focal seizures analyzed. Thalamic ictal activity was present at seizure onset in 81% of sampled thalamic contacts and became nearly universal by seizure termination. Both the thalamus and seizure onset zone showed increased spectral power during seizures, with prominent slow-band augmentation at seizure termination in the thalamus. Similarly, thalamocortical imaginary coherence increased during seizures, with the largest changes near seizure termination in the slow band (AN-SOZ: 11% [IQR, 2 to 20], rank-biserial correlations (rrb) = 0.84; CM-SOZ: 12% [IQR, 3 to 23], rrb = 0.84) and β band (AN-SOZ: 5% [IQR, 0 to 12], rrb = 0.74; CM-SOZ: 8% [IQR, 2 to 15], rrb = 0.86). Directed connectivity analyses demonstrated bidirectional thalamocortical interactions, with large slow-frequency thalamus-to-SOZ outflow near seizure termination from both AN and CM, exceeding propagation-zone-to-SOZ cortico-cortical flow (both p < 0.01). Seizure state was classified using thalamic EEG features, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.825 for AN and 0.839 for CM. Discussion Human focal seizures engage frequency-specific and bidirectional thalamocortical interactions that evolve from onset to termination. These findings support the thalamus as a source of clinically relevant seizure-state information and may inform thalamic biomarker development for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy.

item.title: Age-related changes in brain connectivity: Cross-sectional and longitudinal effects.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Age-related changes in functional connectivity within and between brain networks may contribute to cognitive and behavioral decline in aging. Prior research has consistently reported declines in within-network connectivity with age, though findings on between-network connectivity change have been mixed. Most studies have relied on cross-sectional designs, making it difficult to disentangle age-related effects from confounding cohort effects. Therefore, this study utilizes both cross-sectional (between-subject) and longitudinal (within-subject) datasets and employs mixed-effects models to elucidate age-related changes in resting-state functional connectivity across eight large-scale brain networks. After clinical screening and motion-based quality control, analyses were based on resting-state fMRI from 53 younger adults and 127 older adults, 45 of whom were rescanned approximately 4 years later. We examined whole-brain within-network connectivity, between-network connectivity, and network segregation. Cross-sectionally, older age was associated with lower within-network (p < 0.001) and between-network connectivity (p = 0.003), whereas segregation showed a more modest cross-sectional reduction that was concentrated in the salience and visual networks. Longitudinally, over approximately 4 years both within-network (p = 0.003) and between-network (p = 0.003) connectivity declined, while segregation did not change (p = 0.546). Declines in within- and between-network connectivity were broad rather than network specific, with the Default Mode and Salience networks most consistently affected.

item.title: Hierarchical coding of local and global positions in episodic memory for naturalistic sequences.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Life unfolds continuously across multiple timescales, yet how the brain encodes hierarchical event sequences remains poorly understood. Using magnetoencephalography, we investigated the neural coding of hierarchical positions in naturalistic sequence memory. Participants viewed video sequences with a nested structure and later recalled their serial order. Behavioral analyses revealed transposition errors for items occupying identical global or local position. Multivariate classification and subspace analyses revealed separable neural representations of global and local positions. Local positions were better decoded in sensor space, whereas global positions exhibited greater pattern separability in neural subspace. Brain regions encoding global positions exhibited longer neural timescales, reduced sensitivity to low-level event transitions, and stronger representation for high-level event content, compared to regions encoding local positions. These findings motivate a parallel hierarchical organization of content and context, a novel framework that enables integration of item and order across hierarchical levels and provides principles for hierarchical sequence representation in the brain.

item.title: Immature Valence Recognition of Emotional Speech in Cochlear Implant Users: Evidence From Event-Related Potentials and Neural Oscillations.
item.description:
Ear and hearing
Objectives Rapid emotional perception in speech is crucial to efficient social communication. Cochlear implant (CI) users, constrained by device limitations in transmitting spectro-temporal detail, rely more on semantic than prosodic cues for emotional processing of spoken language. This study investigated whether CI users can rapidly recognize emotional valence based on semantic cues before full semantic comprehension when prosodic information is minimized. Design Chinese monosyllables with negative or positive valence were presented with neutral prosody using an oddball paradigm. Event-related potentials and neural oscillations were recorded in CI users and normal-hearing (NH) listeners. Results Emotional syllables evoked an N400, indicative of semantic processing, in NH listeners. Crucially, NH listeners showed an earlier mismatch negativity (MMN) for negative syllable deviants, reflecting rapid categorical perception of emotional valence. However, the N400 for positive deviants and the MMN were absent in CI users. Furthermore, compared with NH listeners, CI users showed weaker theta-band and alpha-band event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs) and inter-trial coherences and a greater beta-band ERSP. A lower beta-band ERSP was correlated with greater N400 and late negative component in NH listeners. Personality scores for extraversion and agreeableness correlated with the amplitudes of the MMN and N400 components, respectively. Conclusions The findings portray the dynamics of emotional speech processing and demonstrate that rapid recognition of emotional valence expressed by lexical meaning occurs before complete semantic processing in the NH brain. Theta activity may be associated with early emotional valence recognition, and beta activity corresponds to higher-level semantic and emotional processing. However, these two processes are immature in CI users, as evidenced by absent event-related potentials and altered neural oscillations. Personality traits may modulate emotional sensitivity, further affecting the efficiency of emotional speech processing.

item.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
item.description:
Dialogues in clinical neuroscience
Introduction Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. Methods We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Results Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Conclusions Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

item.title: A Neandertal-derived genetic variant reduces occipital brain volume in present-day humans.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neandertal crania were less globular than those of modern humans, suggesting differences in the relative volumes of brain regions, including the frontal and occipital lobes. Here, we show that a common genetic variant influencing occipital brain volume in present-day people was inherited from Neandertals. The variant lies in predicted transcription-factor recognition motifs near DAAM1 , a gene that is known to be involved in brain development. Carriers of the Neandertal variant have altered DAAM1 expression and occipital lobe volumes that are about 0.85 cm³ smaller per gene copy. The variant is associated with reduced schizophrenia risk by almost 10% in homozygous carriers, while Neandertal ancestry as a whole does not show such a tendency. Any association with cognition or schooling is small or nonexistent, amounting to at most two weeks of education per allele against an average of about 15 y. Thus, this Neandertal-derived variant is linked to altered brain anatomy in present-day humans and lower schizophrenia risk while having little or no association with general cognitive ability.

item.title: Transferring active inference to newly encountered prism-shifted environments.
item.description:
Communications biology
Rapid adaptability to sudden changes in environmental contingencies is a hallmark of biological intelligence. However, how animals flexibly adapt to novel environments remains largely unclear. To investigate the brain's generalizability, this work focuses on prism adaptation, a classical visuomotor phenomenon reflecting rapid recalibration of perception-action coupling. Modeling is conducted based on canonical neural networks that instantiate active inference at the circuit level. Namely, we develop canonical neural networks equipped with multiple policy matrices in parallel, enabling the reuse of previously acquired sensorimotor knowledge. We demonstrate that the proposed model recapitulates key features of prism adaptation in an arm-reaching task, including rapid error reduction and after-effects following prism removal. Networks employing policies pretrained for different target positions adapt substantially faster than naive networks that relearn policies from scratch. These results suggest a biologically plausible mechanism by which neural circuits flexibly reuse prior knowledge to support rapid adaptation.

item.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

item.title: Brain predictors of episodic memory change across race/ethnic groups: A machine learning investigation.
item.description:
Neuropsychology
Objective It is known that brain measures predict cognitive trajectories and that these predictions are not uniform across ethnoracial groups. But it remains unclear whether group differences reflect differing brain-cognition associations or similar associations but different demographic and brain health distributions. Method We used eXtreme Gradient Boosting regression tree modeling to predict episodic memory (EM) trajectories from 64 brain measures, including regional gray matter thickness and white matter tract diffusion-tensor free water, with age, sex, education, and ethnoracial indicators in four well-established, ethnically and racially diverse U.S.-based cohorts. eXtreme Gradient Boosting combines many simple regression trees to model nonlinear relationships among predictors and outcome; predictor importance was ranked using SHapley Additive exPlanation values. Results In a sample of 1,463 participants (mean age, 77.0 ± 8.4 years; 503 African American, 168 Asian, 289 Hispanic, and 503 White), a computationally based gray matter signature and white matter tract hippocampal cingulum free-water brain measures ranked first and second in global importance to predict EM trajectory, followed by uncinate fasciculus free water. Generalized additive model analyses by ethnoracial group and age strata showed equivalent pairwise SHapley Additive exPlanation-brain dependency curves for the top two brain measures. Mean absolute deviations were less than 5% of between-participant standard deviation for EM slope, indicating that brain-outcome SHapley Additive exPlanation dependencies were similar across age and ethnoracial groups. Conclusion EM trajectory prediction profiles reflect different sample compositions of brain health measures rather than different brain-EM associations. This suggests that observed variability in brain-EM predictors derives from group-specific distributions of demographic predictors and brain health. item.title: Inter-subject functional variability of gray and white matter during methadone maintenance treatment and its association with gene expression profiles.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Background Methadone maintenance treatment(MMT) for opioid use disorder(OUD) may cause changes in brain functional heterogeneity whose molecular mechanisms remain unknown. This study aims to investigate MMT-related gray/white matter inter-subject variability functional connectivity(GM/WM-IVFC) alterations and to associate them with clinical and transcriptomic characteristics. Methods Between March 2017 and June 2026, a total of 244 participants were voluntarily enrolled from detoxification centers, drug rehabilitation clinics, and society in Hunan Province, China, including MMT group(N = 44), individuals with sustained heroin self-abstinence and no lifetime MMT(HSA, N = 42), short-term abstinent heroin users at baseline(OUD1, N = 62) and 10-month opioid-free follow-up(OUD2, N = 43), and two healthy control cohorts(HC1, N = 48; HC2, N = 48) respectively age/gender-matched with MMT/HSA groups and OUD1. OUD1/2 and HSA groups were used to exploratively investigate the influence of previous heroin use and non-MMT abstinence duration on IVFC. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) data were acquired and analyzed to extract GM/WM-IVFC metrics, which were compared ROI-wise between groups and correlated with neuropsychological scales. Transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas(AHBA) were integrated via partial least squares(PLS) regression and functional enrichment analyses to further identify gene expression profiles underlying IVFC alterations. Results After Bonferroni correction, compared to HC1, MMT group exhibited the most widespread IVFC increases, spanning 20 GM and 7 WM regions. HSA group shared some overlapping GM-IVFC elevations with MMT group in bilateral orbital parts of inferior frontal gyrus and thalamus, yet its overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions was lower than that of MMT group. Neither OUD1 nor OUD2 showed difference in overall mean IVFC of significant GM regions from HC2. Both OUD1/2 displayed elevated overall mean IVFC of significant WM regions relative to HC2. Then, the overall mean IVFC of significant GM/WM regions between MMT group and HC1 were positively correlated with impulsivity, depression, anxiety, insomnia, and daily methadone dose. PLS regression linked IVFC patterns to AHBA transcriptomic profiles in MMT group, with enriched pathways in neuroinflammation, synaptic function, glutamatergic signaling, and neuronal development. Conclusions These findings indicate that MMT is accompanied by cerebral IVFC elevations, whose linkages with neuropsychological aberrations and gene profiles implicate IVFC as a latent clinical phenotype for managing MMT-related complications.

item.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.
